bib.title: SoundStream: An End-to-End Neural Audio Codec

question: Can one end-to-end trained neural codec compress speech, music and general audio at low bitrates better than Opus and EVS, at variable bitrate and low latency?
hypothesis: A learned encoder, residual vector quantizer and adversarially trained decoder beat traditional codecs at low-to-medium bitrates.
contributions: End-to-end trained encoder, decoder, quantizer with reconstruction and adversarial losses
Residual vector quantizer and quantizer dropout for bitrate scalability
Outperforms Opus and EVS across bitrates by subjective tests
Streamable low-latency inference, real time on a smartphone CPU
Joint compression and enhancement with no extra latency

method.summary: Fully convolutional causal SEANet-style encoder, residual vector quantizer (Nq layers, codebook 1024) and decoder, trained jointly with an STFT discriminator and a 3-scale waveform discriminator using hinge adversarial, feature-matching and multi-scale mel reconstruction losses. Quantizer dropout samples nq uniformly in [1,Nq] per example. FiLM conditioning switches denoising on or off.

datasets.name: LibriTTS + Freesound noise
datasets.preprocessing: peak normalisation on random 3 s crops; noise gain uniform in [-30 dB, 0 dB]

datasets.name: Real-world near/far-field speech set
datasets.source: collected by the authors, not released per text

datasets.name: Evaluation set
datasets.size: 200 clips of 2-4 s, 50 from each of 4 datasets

datasets.name: VCTK
datasets.preprocessing: cropped to reduce silence, resampled to 24 kHz, input SNR 0/5/10/15 dB

models.name: SoundStream
models.layers: Benc=Bdec=4 blocks (example given), 3 residual units each, dilation rates 1, 3, and 9

other.strides: (2,4,5,8), M=320 samples, 75 Hz embeddings at 24 kHz, 13.3 ms
other.Nq_max: Nq=8 at 6 kbps; 18 kbps max for scalable

models.name: Lyra
models.architecture: WaveGRU generative codec on mel features, 3 kbps

training.objective: LG = 1*adv(hinge) + 100*feature loss + 1*multi-scale mel reconstruction loss (lambda_adv=1, lambda_feat=100, lambda_rec=1)
training.dropout: quantizer dropout: nq sampled uniformly in [1,Nq]

other.codebook: EMA updates, k-means init on first batch, dead vectors (EMA decay 0.99, threshold 2) replaced by random batch frames
other.mel_loss: scales s=2^6..2^11, 64-bin mel, hop s/4, alpha_s=sqrt(s/2)

inference.decoding: deterministic encode/decode; nq chosen from desired bitrate

other.rtf: measured on single CPU thread of Pixel4

metrics.name: MUSHRA-inspired score
metrics.definition: crowd-sourced, hidden reference, no anchor, 20 ratings per clip; native English speakers with headphones; screened out raters scoring reference <90 over 20% or non-reference >90 over 50%

metrics.name: ViSQOL
metrics.definition: open-source objective quality metric used for model selection and ablations

metrics.name: RTF
metrics.definition: ratio of input audio length to time needed to encode/decode

availability.data: audio examples on a public webpage (google-research.github.io/seanet/soundstream/examples/)

results.claim: SoundStream at 3 kbps is matched only by EVS at 9.6 kbps and Opus at 12 kbps (3.2x to 4x more bits).
results.setup: MUSHRA-inspired crowdsourced test, 200 clips, 20 ratings each, 24 kHz
results.quote: To match the quality of SoundStream, EVS needs to use at least 9.6 kbps and Opus at least 12 kbps, i.e., 3.2× to 4× more bits than SoundStream.

results.claim: At 6 kbps, EVS and Opus need 2.2x to 2.6x more bits to match SoundStream.
results.quote: At medium bitrates, EVS and Opus require, respectively, 2.2× to 2.6× more bits to match the same quality.

results.claim: At 12 kbps, 1.3x to 1.6x more bits are needed by the baselines.
results.quote: At high bitrates, 1.3× to 1.6× more bits.

results.claim: ViSQOL stays above 3.7 across 3 to 18 kbps.
results.setup: Test data, all four content types, SoundStream at constant bitrate
results.quote: it remains above 3.7 even at the lowest bitrate

results.claim: Entropy coding could save 7% to 20% of bitrate.
results.setup: Empirical entropy of RVQ symbols, memoryless source assumption
results.quote: Figure 7a indicates a potential rate saving between 7% and 20%.

results.claim: Replacing the learned encoder with a fixed mel filterbank drops ViSQOL from 3.96 to 3.33 at 6 kbps.
results.setup: 6 kbps, quantizer and decoder still learned

results.claim: Learned encoder at 3 kbps (half the bitrate) still beats the mel-encoder model at 6 kbps.
Quantizer dropout closes the quality gap of one model across bitrates; scalable model marginally beats bitrate-specific models at 9 and 12 kbps.
results.setup: ViSQOL, model trained at 18 kbps with dropout vs without vs bitrate-specific, Fig 7c

results.claim: Default model (Cenc=Cdec=32, 8.4M params) runs in real time on one Pixel4 CPU thread.
results.setup: Pixel4 single CPU thread, 6 kbps, ViSQOL 4.01

results.claim: Smaller encoder (Cenc=8, Cdec=32) gives encoder RTF 18.6x with ViSQOL 3.99.
Smaller decoder (Cdec=8) costs more quality: ViSQOL 3.90.
80 one-bit quantizers at 6 kbps give ViSQOL 3.92 vs 4.01 for 8 x 1024.
Architectural latency of 7.5/13/26 ms gives equal ViSQOL 4.01 at 6 kbps but higher RTF with more latency.
One joint compression and enhancement model is near the disjoint SEANet+SoundStream pipelines on VCTK, at half the compute.

limits: Optimizer, learning rate, batch size, steps, hardware and dataset sizes are not stated, so training cannot be rerun from the paper.
Constant bitrate only; entropy coding savings are an estimate (lower bound), not implemented.
Evaluation clips are 2 to 4 seconds long; ViSQOL is the objective metric, MUSHRA only for main comparison.
Real-world evaluation set was collected by the authors and no release is stated.

terms.definition: Residual (multi-stage) vector quantizer cascading Nq VQ layers over successive residuals
sample nq uniformly in [1;Nq] per example and only use quantizers Qi for i = 1 . . . nq

lineage.note: learnable vector quantizer extended to residual
multi-scale waveform discriminator and feature loss
